I'm going to (try to) be polite and assume this is the first time you've encountered articles about US gun laws, so here goes:

There Is No Such Thing As An Assault Weapon.

There are assault rifles, which are either select-fire or automatic-only. These are not banned, but they closed the registry to register new ones in 1986. This has caused their price to skyrocket as there is a fixed amount that will exist so long as the Hughes Amendment stands. To purchase one (assuming you have the money) you must pay a $200 additional tax and pass a stringent background check by the FBI (this is in addition to the standard NICS check that any purchase through an FFL must go through).

Semi-auto only guns that look like assault rifles are just modern sporting (also called 'tactical') rifles. These differ from a semi-auto "ranch rifle" in cosmetics and ergonomics only. They're still only 1 bullet per trigger pull no matter how hard you hold the trigger down. These were heavily restricted from 1994-2004 by the Clinton "Assault Weapons" Ban, a law that had absolutely zero effect on crime or mass-shootings.

I know it may seem pedantic to argue semantics and terminology but the anti-gun groups intentionally abuse language to make things seem much worse and scarier than they are to drum up support for their campaigns. The best way to combat this is to be a stickler on terminology to make sure that those on the outside looking in understand what's actually being discussed.

Around here you can bill people up to 20k$ or 30k$ a year before needing sales tax registration. So if it's below that, hire them as a contractor. You get a bunch of bills to deduct & they get to deduct expenses as self employed, even if it's part time... win-win

Quebec/Canada

Well, this is just a guide-line, your state/county/country will change these rules slightly:

You will have to keep a running record of the wages and times the employee worked, preferably a time-sheet they can sign every day to verify the times are correct. You keep these records for both tax purposes, and for legal issues ( in case they claim they are owed more in a paycheck etc.).

When it comes to taxes, just follow the IRS's guide, since they are the ones who care anyhow.

As far as other legal matters go, if there is any, and I mean ANY remote possibility of the employee becoming injured on the job (that includes tripping and falling) you might want to look into some kind of insurance policy (they are pretty expensive, but if you don't know the worker, or it's a particularly risky job, it can save your ass. )

Also, I hope you are registered as a Limited Liability Corporation, else, if something happens, they can sue you directly, rather than just the business entity.
